caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: UK debt went from 41.9% of GDP in 2006 (the series low) to 104.8% in 2020, the series peak, via the financial crisis, austerity-era stagnation, and COVID. It fell to 97.5% in 2022 and is projected at 102.3% in 2025 — essentially flat for five years, as deficits persist. GDP grew from $2,723.4bn in 2006 to a projected $4,003.0bn in 2025. The UK borrows in its own currency with deep markets, so sustainability is about the fiscal path, not market access; but the 2022 gilt crisis showed that credibility is not automatic. Debt interest is now among the highest in the G7 as a share of revenue.
inflation_management: The Bank of England targets 2%, and its record divides at Brexit and the energy shock: 2.2% in 2009, 0% in 2015 (the low), 0.9% in 2020, then 9.1% in 2022, the series high — the G7's worst, driven by energy dependence and a tight labor market. It fell to 2.5% in 2024 but is projected at 3.4% for 2025, the highest in the G7, as regulated energy prices and wage growth kept it elevated. The Bank was criticized for hiking late, then held rates higher for longer; the 2025 overshoot shows the last mile is the hardest. Sterling's post-Brexit weakness has been a persistent imported-inflation channel.

key_events.event: Financial crisis: bank nationalizations (Northern Rock, RBS) ended the low-debt era.
Austerity era under the coalition government; debt climbed steadily through the 2010s.
Brexit referendum (June 2016); formal exit (January 2020) reshaped trade and labor supply.
COVID-19: debt hit 104.8% of GDP, the series peak, on the contraction and furlough spending.
Mini-budget gilt crisis (September 2022): credibility shock; inflation hit 9.1%.
Inflation projected at 3.4%, the G7's highest; debt projected at 102.3% of GDP.

outlook_next_decade: The UK's outlook is constrained by the twin overhangs of Brexit and debt: trend growth has slowed, the fiscal position needs consolidation from 102% of GDP, and inflation is proving stickier than peers'. The new government's growth agenda — planning reform, investment — is the upside lever; delivery is unproven. The analytical assessment: the UK retains deep advantages (services, finance, universities, its own currency), but the last decade's shocks have left it with less fiscal room and a credibility deficit to rebuild. Debt sustainability is fine; the cost of the debt is the problem.
